Document · 1994

On Completing Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind

Hayao Miyazaki · 1 June 1994
Yomu (To Read), Iwanami Shoten, June 1994 · from Starting Point: 1979–1996, Hayao Miyazaki (VIZ Media, 2009)

The Story Continues

Yomu (To Read), Iwanami Shoten, June 1994

A work I wasn’t sure I could complete

—You’ve finally finished serializing the manga version of Nausicaä of the Valley of the Wind, after a total of thirteen years, haven’t you …

Miyazaki: Well, there were fifty-nine episodes, which itself amounts to five years, but I spent time on the story before and after that, too, so the total amount spent on it probably means that during the last twelve or thirteen years, I was actually busy working on Nausicaä about half the time, in some form or another.

In the beginning, it was a work that I wasn’t sure I could complete. But since I had decided that I could stop working on it at any point, you could also say that I was able to create the story without worrying about the future. I was able to work on it without just hoping to make it this or that way—I was able to really impose my will on it.

—That’s interesting. To me it seemed to be almost like one of the long-running period dramas they serialize on NHK TV—a fictional work of such grand scale that it requires a very meticulous organization from beginning to end, and takes a great deal of time to write very carefully.

Miyazaki: There’s no way that I would have been capable of that sort of organization. I was always under the pressure of lots of tight deadlines; several times I didn’t realize until much later the true significance of what I had actually written.

—In 1984, three years after starting the serialization of Nausicaä, the animated film was released, and now, exactly ten years later, you’ve finally finished drawing the manga. In the interim, the work has been evaluated and critiqued from all sorts of angles, hasn’t it?

Miyazaki: Yes, and some people who had first seen the film apparently went back and read the manga version from that perspective. Some who first saw Nausicaä as an ecological warrior were therefore never able to think of her as anything beyond that. Of course, I suppose you could say, conversely, that the manga wasn’t sufficiently powerful to move them beyond that impression …

—There is quite a difference between the film and manga versions, isn’t there? In the manga version you get a better idea of the more complex aspects of Nausicaä’s personality.

Miyazaki: Yes, of course. If the film version and manga version were the same, it would’ve been ridiculous to keep drawing the manga story after the film ended.

I didn’t have enough confidence in the direction of the manga story when I resumed it after the film; there were aspects of the film story that I wasn’t able to shake off, and I really had to force myself to continue. To be more honest, I should say that when I had to temporarily stop work on the manga serialization in order to make my next film, I felt such a huge sense of relief that it was almost as though I had fled from my desk.

It’s not something I’m proud to say, but when work on the next film ended, even after I had taken a bit of a break, I still found it agonizing to go back to the Nausicaä manga. I ultimately wound up stopping the serialization four times.

—And the film version wound up becoming the flag-bearer for the ecology movement that was so popular in the 1980s …

Miyazaki: That wasn’t intended at all; I think that Nausicaä just happened to be in the right place at the right time to play that role. I’d actually been thinking about such issues much earlier, and had gotten my start with them thanks in part to books by the botanist Sasuke Nakao.

What I mean to say is that I didn’t start out writing and drawing Nausicaä because I specifically wanted to talk about ecosystems or the need to protect the environment. I started out intending to set the story in the desert, but when I drew some illustrations they weren’t very interesting, so then I came up with the idea of setting the story in a forest, and that seemed to make more sense. So I ultimately wound up with the story that you know today.

So this is yet another example of how I created a story without having a big, overriding plan. I wrote it thinking that maybe I should go in this or that direction, and then just followed my whim. When I got stuck, I tried to put something big into the story and came up with the idea of the long-sleeping kyoshinhei, or giant god-soldiers … This was just something I came up with when I was in a pickle and didn’t know where to take the story. I kept deceiving myself in order to keep going; I felt that everything would probably work out all right and that besides, the magazine in which the story was being serialized would probably do me a favor and go out of business before I got to the end anyway … [laughs]

—What sort of story did you intend to create when you first set it in the desert?

Miyazaki: I don’t remember. I’m sure that I must have been thinking of all sorts of things, but I really don’t remember … One thing I do remember well, however, is that I was extremely irritated at the time. I confess I was angry about the general state of the world, among other things.

—This was around 1981 or 1982, wasn’t it?

Miyazaki: It was right around 1980. In addition to being upset by environmental problems, I was also concerned about where humanity was headed, and especially about the state of Japan. Most of all, I suspect, I was angered by the state of my own self.

—So right at the peak of the economic bubble you were …

Miyazaki: I was embarrassed. I was disgusted. I wish I could say that I’m over it now, but my feelings of gloom have just shifted to other areas.

Feeling cornered after finishing the film

—If it’s true that you didn’t really have a framework for the entire story until you finished it, it must have been tough for you when you actually got the go ahead for the Nausicaä film project.

Miyazaki: Frankly, I was really in a fix. I could have aggressively attacked the problem if the film had been based on someone else’s work, but it was my own work, something that I had been cooking up until that point. It was almost impossible for me to be objective about it. Even if not explicitly written or drawn in the original manga story, there were many personal feelings—as well as my own wild ideas—in every panel of every page. So I just took what was in the original manga story as motifs, changed their meaning, rearranged them, put them into a Japanese furoshiki-wrapping cloth, so to speak, and tried to make them fit as best I could.

For films, you have to untie the furoshiki to show people what you have inside; then you also have to tie it up again. Now, I know that some people say that with films you can just leave the furoshiki untied, but I’m in the entertainment business, so I have to think about what fits and what doesn’t.

That’s all you can do with film. It’s important that Nausicaä, the heroine, discover the real role, structure, and significance of the fukai, or Sea of Decay, and as a result trigger a Copernican-like revolution in understanding. I had decided that was about all I could show in a film version, but there were too many elements still in my mind that wouldn’t fit into that simplified framework and it bothered me that I couldn’t make them work.

It’s no wonder that there were problems, because in the manga I essentially decided to write about whatever I wasn’t able to depict in the film.

—That makes sense. So that’s why the film and the manga book versions are clearly two different works. Because, as with a furoshiki, with a film there’s a specific way that the story has to be opened and then tied-up, isn’t there?

Miyazaki: I’ve finally finished serializing the manga version now, but even if I had to go back and redo everything and make the film first, I’m sure I would make the same thing. There would be no changes.

—Do you think the way you ended the film influenced the way you later ended the manga story?

Miyazaki: As I indicated before, films have an “end mark,” or clear ending, so I didn’t keep creating the manga story in an attempt to follow the film’s story. I frankly didn’t worry about what I had done in the film at all. Mainly because I’d already forgotten most of it. [laughs]

Yet, especially in the initial stages of making the Nausicaä film, I kept insisting that the story only represented a wish on my part, that I wasn’t working from any assumed reality. But when the film was finished I discovered that I was actually up to my neck in the religious zone I had always wanted to avoid; I seriously felt that I had backed myself into a corner, and thought, “Uh-oh …”

On finishing the film I told myself that if I were going to continue the manga serialization I would have to take a more no-nonsense approach. While creating the manga, however, I also realized there were so many things I didn’t understand that I would have to keep going without ever figuring them out.

—You wrote far more of the manga story after finishing the film than before, didn’t you …

Miyazaki: Yes. And as a result, there was probably a changeover of readers. I also worried that my readers wouldn’t have a clue what was going on, even if they did follow the whole story as serialized in the magazine. But I still wound up pondering too many imponderables.

—What do you mean?

Miyazaki: If you assume that there is a God, you can explain everything in the world. But I can’t do that. Still, in Nausicaä I wound up entering a zone that I didn’t particularly want to enter, about humans and life and so forth.

I can more or less understand the world from the perspective of human conflicts and contradictions, but there’s a part of me dissatisfied by that sort of explanation alone. So that means there’s nothing that I can say with much conviction about anything at all.

I started to get dizzy just thinking about what I would do if addressed as “mama” by something with the destructive power of the kyoshinhei. So Nausicaä’s confusion is also my own confusion.

—The kyoshinhei, or giant god-soldier, plays a totally different role in the ending of the manga story than it does in the film …

Miyazaki: In popular culture, there are countless examples of characters coming upon some giant thing that gives them power. This “thing” may take the form of elephant herds in Tarzan, or the robot in Tetsujin 28-go (Gigantor). And what we see appearing over and over again in different forms can be explained as a human desire for a larger existence than oneself or a desire for growth. In popular culture the true nature of a giant force is often depicted vaguely, but it is ideally a good force.

In reality, most power has probably been created by technology. I think that technology is by itself neutral, innocent. It’s like the automobile. Automobiles are extremely loyal to their drivers, and self-sacrificing, too.

It may be safe to assume that machines don’t have souls, but in reality people impart souls to machines. Just as a dog will obey the orders of its master no matter how evil that master may be, the essence of a machine is its loyalty, devotion, and self-sacrifice. I think that this concept of humans imparting souls to machines is at the core, for example, of Isaac Asimov’s famous “Three Laws of Robotics.” The basic concept behind the kyoshinhei in Nausicaä is therefore really a very ordinary one. You can even find countless prior examples that illustrate the roots of the design. But the moment I made the kyoshinhei pure or innocent in a visible way, it got out of my control. And I probably made it that way because I, too, have an intense fascination with things pure and innocent …

—After the kyoshinhei gained consciousness, the story began developing into something quite different, didn’t it?

Miyazaki: When creating a work like Nausicaä, all sorts of ideas, even random fragments of ideas, come to me. I just have to assume that they mean something. I can’t ignore these fragments even if they might destroy the story structure. I know I’m not explaining this very well.

Whatever I may think, I’m sure someone else has already spoken about it long, long ago, with greater depth and insight and more appropriate language. In writing Nausicaä, I became painfully aware of my lack of ability in this area.

—Do you mean the ability to talk about the religious area you found yourself getting into?

Miyazaki: It seems to me that many of the attributes of the human mind, including the beliefs and convictions we think important, may actually exist in nature …

Bonnō, or worldly desires, may emerge in our minds as a scrambled mess, but if we want to transcend them and arrive at a true, purer state of being, then I have this terrifying sense of foreboding that we might wind up as plain old pebbles or drops of water.

Yet the moment one starts talking about this sort of thing, it immediately starts to sound like a very annoying and even sinister religion. I’ve never reached this state of consciousness, and there’s no way I could write about it properly anyway. In short, after a while, the kyoshinhei started to seem even more charming to me than the humans.

—Sort of the way the ohmu start seeming more endearing … I know there are also other, similar examples in the manga version of Nausicaä.

I was at a loss for words

Miyazaki: I’m still confused, because I tend to get hung up on things like that. Sometimes I think it’s like Dr. Strangelove, or maybe that it’s just truly abnormal. I really don’t know.

The world’s simplest viruses may share with us what we think of as uniquely human emotions, etc. In our case, do these qualities just happen to be accidentally invoked in human form? When I start thinking about this, I feel that I need to do some religious training and develop some more advanced gray matter. If not, I might wander into an area that probably shouldn’t be verbalized.

I really got bogged down in Nausicaä with this sort of thinking. I knew it was dangerous, but I felt compelled to take the story in the direction I did because ten years earlier I had started using the kyoshinhei character. And I couldn’t get away with saying that I’d used it and then just forgotten about it. [laughs]

So in effect, I myself wasn’t in the lead in creating this story; I was just trying to keep up with it.

—So you’re saying that the story started rolling on its own?

Miyazaki: Rather than rolling on its own, I should say that the story took on a life of its own. And it wouldn’t agree to go where I wanted it to go. Of course, while realizing that I wasn’t being very honest about it all, I still felt forced to try to get the story to go where I wanted it to, but that’s not something I recommend.

Ultimately, the question is whether the young heroine, Nausicaä, who has the weight of the world on her shoulders, can ever truly return to a normal life. Can she really go on living without losing her mind? The only thing I know is that she probably will never be able to go back to being the way she was, but that she can definitely continue as she has become, that she can be a witness to what has happened.

—There’s a certain resolution to the story in the animated film, but in the beginning of the manga version Nausicaä poses a variety of questions. The number of questions keeps increasing, and the story ends with them still unresolved.

Miyazaki: That’s true. There were many questions—such as the meaning of life—that from the beginning I knew couldn’t be resolved, but it turned out that I couldn’t avoid asking them.

My dog is sixteen-and-a-half years old, and so worn out that we wouldn’t be surprised if he passed away any day now. He has cataracts so bad that he can hardly see, he can barely smell, and he barely hears out of one ear. But he’s still alive. When I look at his face, I often suspect that he’s not particularly happy, but when I offer to take him for a walk, he lights up quite a bit.

It makes me wonder what it means to be alive. Both of my parents have already passed away, so it may seem a bit twisted to say that I think such thoughts when I look at my dog, but sometimes I wonder if he’s really the same dog as the one who used to be here. Perhaps it’s sort of like ripples spreading on the surface of water. The farther out the ripples travel, the fainter they become—they are still ripples, but they are not the same as they once were, when first generated and full of energy.

Some people say living things are, among other things, merely carriers of “selfish genes,” but that’s ultimately not enough of an explanation for me. All I can say is that we’re just at the beginning of figuring all this out, and that I suspect wise old people in ancient times probably sensed such things, and spent a lot of time thinking about them, long before there was any formal field of study of them.

—So in other words, you begin to understand how much you don’t understand …

Miyazaki: Yes. You realize that, whether talking about the relationship between man and nature, or the nature that exists within man, there is no single easy answer to any of it. To live means to have a method of maintaining an easy balance, so that all you can do is say that one should or should not do something for the sake of maintaining that balance.

But if you take this logic a step further, you soon run into problems that require confronting the chaotic dark side of the universe, and when it gets to that point, I think the answers lie not with our modern brains, but with what the ancients pondered in their mountain retreats not too long ago.

Recently, I find myself being shocked by religious language that I never used to pay much attention to. I feel as though I understand what it is trying to say. I sense, for example, that behind the very simple writings in an introductory Buddhist text or oft-spoken religious words, there are truly incredible experiences and ideas. But if you ask me if I have absorbed these ideas, the answer is no, I merely live in awe of them.

The moment you start transcribing words they start transforming themselves; unlike the Buddhist sage Shinran or others who fearlessly wrote down such words, I decided not to give Nausicaä any similar lines. Had I done so they would have sounded fake.

I had intended to organize my thoughts to have a better grasp of things, but in the process of writing Nausicaä I lost control; I felt like I was at a loss for words. It was almost as though Nausicaä herself were at a loss for words. I felt that I didn’t want to express myself in words; whenever I wrote down something that I thought probably expressed my intent, it immediately turned into something else.

—So after Nausicaä resolves to tell what is in effect a lie, the story soon comes to a conclusion …

Miyazaki: That somehow seemed more appropriate for my heroine, so that’s the way it turned out. The only way to look at it is to understand that her “lie” is an expression of her love for the life around her.

At any rate, it would be false to say that because we’re on the side of justice, we can go ahead and destroy our opponents and the world will be at peace. That, at least, I can say would be a total lie. Now, I know that there are such things as good and evil in the world, and that people do good things. But people who do good things are not necessarily good people, they just happen to be people who have done good things. The next instant they might wind up doing something bad, and if we don’t take that into account in our view of humans, we’ll constantly make mistakes when making political decisions or decisions about ourselves.

The collapse of the Soviet Union came even more unexpectedly than that of the Dorok nation

—Many big events happened during the long serialization of the Nausicaä manga, both within Japan and in the wider world. Did any of them influence you?

Miyazaki: The most shocking thing to me was the civil war in Yugoslavia.

—What do you mean by that?

Miyazaki: I just didn’t think the people there would resort to that sort of thing. It’s a place where so many terrible things have been done in the past, I thought they would have had enough of it, but apparently they haven’t. It taught me that people never do have enough of anything, that I was naïve.

—Compared to the Gulf War, it has been a fairly traditional war, hasn’t it?

Miyazaki: Yes, the Gulf War was in a sense fairly easy to understand. There were actually a lot of similarities between the Iraqi government and the government in Japan when it was controlled by a military clique. Like when our military used to send troops to some ridiculously out of the way island or desert and abandon them there, without water or food, and tell them to fend for themselves. Looking at the Iraqi military was painful, almost like looking at Japan’s former military, but the situation in Yugoslavia is completely different.

I think the people who started everything in Yugoslavia were probably just a few gangster types, but no one could stop them. It probably resembled Germany when the Nazis emerged and most of the people just saw them as a bunch of thugs, but then suddenly found that the Nazis had grown into an unstoppable force.

If you just watched a news source like CNN, you would think that the Serbs are overwhelmingly bad. But there is something completely different at work there. Within Christianity, there is clearly bad blood between the West and the Eastern Orthodox Church. So it was inevitable that the Serbs would be skeptical of NATO’s moves. They probably would be relieved if Russia were more involved.

But that doesn’t mean that the Serbs are in the right. Both sides are truly foolish, and both are doing horrible things. The thing about war is that even though people may have a sense of what is just in the beginning, once you start a war that sense of justice inevitably becomes corrupted.

—Nausicaä herself says that there is no such thing as justice, doesn’t she?

Miyazaki: I’m fascinated by wars, and I read a lot about them. People therefore often ask me, “Miyazaki-san, do you like war?” and I respond by asking if they think AIDS researchers like AIDS. Either way, the conflict in Yugoslavia has taught me that my understanding of history was completely naïve.

—What do you think about the collapse of the Soviet Union, which triggered the conflict in Yugoslavia?

Miyazaki: The Soviet Union collapsed while I was still serializing the Nausicaä manga and writing about the collapse of the Dorok empire. I was actually marveling at how suddenly the Dorok nation fell apart in my own story, and then the Soviet Union collapsed even more suddenly, which really shocked me.

It taught me that nations can collapse and people can keep on living their lives as ever, and that both things can quite easily occur at the same time. I had always wondered what had happened when the Roman empire collapsed, and what sort of changes the people living there might have experienced, and with the collapse of the Soviet Union I now feel as though I have an idea.

—I see. It was really quite a coincidence, wasn’t it?

Miyazaki: Yes, and I actually should have written many more details about the collapse of the Dorok empire into the Nausicaä story, but sixteen pages a month was my measly physical limit, so I had to leave out a lot. I kept thinking, while drawing, that I should explain why Dorok collapsed, what a country really is, what sort of system Dorok had, how that system stopped functioning, and so forth, and while worrying about running out of time, in the manga story the Dorok empire collapsed all on its own, just like, in the real world, the Soviet Union did.

Nausicaä changed my way of thinking

Miyazaki: As I was trying to complete Nausicaä, I experienced a change in my thinking that some people might regard as a political sell-out. It’s because I clearly abandoned Marxism. You might say I had to abandon it, but it wasn’t easy to decide that Marxism was a mistake, that Marxist materialism was all wrong, that I had to look at the world in a different way. I still occasionally think it would have been easier for me to continue thinking as I had been.

I didn’t experience any dramatic, fierce internal struggle before changing my way of thinking; I was simply no longer able to deal with the various doubts that had been accumulating as I wrote. And I don’t think I abandoned Marxism because of any change in my position within society—on the contrary, I feel that it came from having written Nausicaä.

For example, I felt a little hesitation in the beginning simply because I had made Nausicaä the daughter of Jihl, the king of a small nation, which therefore made her a princess. Anticipating that some people might criticize my heroine for belonging to an elite class, I armed myself with all sorts of theories to defend myself. But after a while I no longer cared about that. Nausicaä could have been born anywhere. I have no intention of arguing about it at all. No matter what class people are born into, idiots are still idiots and good people are still good. It’s not just about right or wrong in this world; people are either good or not, people we want to have as friends or not. I’ve resolved not to think of things in terms of class consciousness. The idea that someone’s right just because he’s a worker is a lie. The masses are capable of doing an infinite number of stupid things. And I certainly don’t trust public opinion polls.

So with all this, we simply wind up back at a very ordinary place. I’m not talking about something as profound as having had the scales fall from my eyes, but if I think of my new state of mind as returning to believing just what I’ve been told over and over again, then it does seem depressing. However, it is something I have to accept. I have simply resolved to take responsibility for the way I see the world.

Around the end of the 1950s, when I first saw a film about Mao Zedong standing in Tiananmen Square to the acclaim of the masses, he seemed to have a truly ominous, ugly look to him. But since he was always described as really being a big-hearted, warm man, I thought that, well, perhaps he hadn’t been feeling well, or that maybe the photography hadn’t been very good. [laughs] Looking back on it, though, I should have trusted my first impression.

That sort of thing has happened several times to me. Using my own sense of what’s proper, I’ve twisted and suppressed my initial subjective impressions. Well, I don’t do that anymore. Even when looking at today’s politicians, I just rely on my impressions.

—So you rely on your intuition …

Miyazaki: Rather than call it intuition, I just have a sense that this or that person is a good person. Even if they don’t have much ability as a politician, I might feel that they are basically good. And since I know I can’t really expect much of them anyway, I’d rather just pick the best person of the bunch. That’s the level that I’ve finally come to, and the only way I feel comfortable thinking of things. In other words, I’ve reverted to being a true simpleton.

—Perhaps it’s not a matter of reverting, but having climbed a long spiral staircase?

Miyazaki: But I sometimes feel as though I’m just spiraling around … Take the Totoro Forest Project movement, for example. The people in the movement are using a film character that we created, but I don’t support what they’re doing because they’re “right.” I support them because they are really good people. They’re really doing good, steady work.

Long before the movement started, these were people who loved the Sayama hills and walked through them whenever they could to admire the fauna and the birds, and they wondered if they couldn’t do something to preserve the area. And because the movement comprises this sort of people, I felt it would be all right for them to use our characters. Believe me, if they were a bunch of ecology fascists, we’d quit helping them.

So this is an example of how I now try to interact with people; not on the basis of whether they are correct or not, but whether they are good people or not. Of course, as a result, my world has been getting smaller and smaller. [laughs]

An environmental problem solved by cleaning the neighboring river

—Can you comment on what about Japan angered you so much before you started to draw Nausicaä?

Miyazaki: I personally feel so much better now; I’m long past the stage of feeling that Japan got what it deserved after the economic bubble burst. None of the big problems have been solved, of course, but now the walls have come down and the outside world’s coming in. People moan about a shortage of domestically produced rice, but it’s really nothing. It’s not as though we’re starving to death. I’ve actually been more amazed by our economic power.

—You mean that we can buy whatever we want today?

Miyazaki: Well, if we’d had a shortage of rice around 1945, it would’ve been a huge problem, but today the main issue is people complaining about rice imported from Thailand not tasting as good and so forth, so I think we’ve got enormous underlying strengths now. At the same time, it makes me realize how hard it is for countries in the world that don’t have much economic power …

At the risk of being misunderstood, let me say that I’m getting sick of hearing everyone arguing about the state of Japanese agriculture. I happen to know a farmer who continues to grow rice organically, without using pesticides, and I decided to sign a contract with him to grow rice for us, even if we have to pay more money for it when there is a poor harvest. That solved the agricultural problems for my family. [laughs]

Of course, this doesn’t provide any sort of solution in the larger sense; I can understand the anger behind sensational statements like, “Japan’s agricultural industry has lost!” but I’m frankly just as sick of hearing that as I am of hearing people say, “The Japanese film industry has been ruined!” It seems to me that people are missing the point. We’re not talking here about issues where words like “winning” or “losing” really apply. I just get more and more irritated when I hear people going on and on about agricultural problems, or this or that aspect of the nation’s Agricultural Cooperatives. My position isn’t a popular one, but I say we’d be better off solving far more personal problems. I would, of course, think differently if there really were a danger of people starving to death …

I find that I can only deal with these sorts of issues on a local level. In terms of the environment, some people in the area where I live have been trying to clean up the local river, so when I have the time, I help out, and I think that sort of contribution ought to be okay. Now, I’m just talking about picking up plastic bags people have thrown away, and that sort of thing, so I’m fully aware that it doesn’t yield any fundamental solution to our problems.

What I’m trying to say here is that if we’re mainly confining ourselves to big-picture, general statements about things, there’s simply too much beyond our control. One reason we humans have so many problems, I’m convinced, is precisely because there is this huge disjunction between the world of generalized statements and the world of specifics, or details. But humans can be perfectly satisfied by working with the details. It’s an idea that I recently find very appealing.

If you only think of problems from the big-picture level—as if looking down from a mountain or an airplane—they may seem to be truly unsolvable. But if you get closer to the ground, you may see a path to solve them that proceeds fifty meters or so. It may look like an appealing road, and if the weather’s good and the sun’s out you may feel energized and able to make it down the road. The point that intrigues me here is that by merely changing your perspective your thoughts on an issue may change as well.

So for me, rather than pontificating from a lectern at some symposium or lecture, I’d rather be engaged in the sort of activities I’ve mentioned. I’m going to keep irresponsibly saying whatever I want, and for those determined to keep driving and spewing out pollution, and those who insist on driving until everyone else quits, or are determined to be the last drivers on the roads, well, they really ought to raise the price of gasoline to three hundred yen a liter. [laughs]

—If they do that, the number of cars would really drop, wouldn’t it?

Miyazaki: Yes, and I get really upset when I hear people say that we should stimulate the Japanese economy by reducing the price of gasoline. People who are determined at all costs to drive cars should drive them. But the idea that everyone should drive a car doesn’t represent human progress or contribute to equality at all.

In many areas today, mass popularization has become a bit of a problem. To give you an example, when I look at an old photograph of a zeppelin airship, it makes me realize how much I would have loved to have flown in one. But if I think about it objectively, because I’m presumably a bona fide member of the ordinary masses, I also know that during the actual age of zeppelins my kind of people probably couldn’t have ever bought a ticket. Yet that doesn’t mean I think we ought to go out and create an age where everyone can ride in a zeppelin.

At Studio Ghibli, we’re thinking of installing sod on the roof of the building and planting grass this year. Doing so won’t solve any of the world’s problems, but it feels better than just getting angry, and I’m told that it may reduce our heating and air conditioning bills. Of course, lots of people would say it won’t solve anything at all, and they may well be right, but it’s at least something we can do, so I just want to try it.

I know a cameraman who started a movement to bring children who had been exposed to radiation at Chernobyl to Japan for treatment. Simply bringing them to Japan for a month or so and giving them nutritious food, among other things, apparently makes them much healthier. Some kids who’ve stopped growing apparently even start growing again.

Now, the cameraman I’m talking about knows that if the children go back home after a month here, they’ll probably revert to their former condition. So he’s troubled by the thought that even if he does manage to bring a dozen or so kids to Japan, he won’t be able to do anything to help the tens of thousands of others still left behind. At the risk of being misunderstood, though, I think that what he is doing is fine, because he is doing what he is capable of doing, and that’s really all we can do. Now, some people might say that if one of the kids goes back and dies it would negate the meaning of what the man is doing, but I would say no. If that were to happen, I think everything would revolve around what that particular child felt. But anything you can say about this personal level of activism can potentially be terribly misunderstood. It’s a difficult problem. If you try to form an opinion about something like this based purely on results, everything becomes very problematic. If I say that the moment we are living in is the most important, then I could be misinterpreted as advocating merely living for the moment in an irresponsible way, so that becomes difficult, too. Everything becomes difficult when you put it in words.

—Words are easy to interpret in different ways, aren’t they? No matter what you say, people can find fault with it.

Miyazaki: There are a lot of things I simply can’t put into words. To give you an example of how hard it is, if I say that all one needs to do is to clean up a river, then plenty of people will immediately brand me as someone with the government-approved Eco Mark.

—It sounds like a bit of a sore point for you.

Miyazaki: It is. Because I really don’t want to say anything about this sort of thing. It’d be much easier just to shut up. It’s much easier for me to just do things like this as part of being a good neighbor.

I’ve decided to accept what I don’t understand as unknowns

—After you finished the Nausicaä film but were still serializing the manga story, you managed to create animated features like Castle in the Sky, My Neighbor Totoro, Kiki’s Delivery Service, and Porco Rosso. These are all quite different from Nausicaä, aren’t they?

Miyazaki: I actually feel as though working on Nausicaä may have made it possible for me to create those films. Of all of these works, Nausicaä weighed the heaviest on my shoulders. Going back to the world of Nausicaä after stopping work on it was so difficult that I found myself not wanting to. In fact, although I was obviously writing it while living in the real world, working on Nausicaä made it difficult to reintegrate into society.

—You mean that you find yourself becoming more and more withdrawn?

Miyazaki: Yes. When I’m working on a film production, everything’s chaotic, as you can imagine. There are lots and lots of truly stupid, ordinary things that I have to deal with. I find myself living in a truly crude world, thinking, “Hey, why’s that guy loafing?” or, “Why doesn’t he hurry up and get married and settle down?” [laughs] And I find myself trying to work, whether the theaters showing our films are jammed with crowds or not.

After my work on the films ended, and I was feeling dazed and wanted to take a break, I always had the Nausicaä manga waiting for me. This is what I really hated. I would usually spend about six months doing everything to avoid Nausicaä, and then, finally, because I had no other choice, eventually start working on it again. So to tell you the truth, as I mentioned earlier, it was almost as if I’d been creating films just to avoid Nausicaä.

I won’t go so far as to say that because I had something as heavy as Nausicaä to work on, I deliberately created lighter works. I do think, however, that if I hadn’t had Nausicaä to work on I probably would have been floundering about, trying to incorporate somewhat more serious elements into the films. Of course, I can only say this in hindsight; at the time I didn’t feel this way, and just made such films because I thought it was the right thing to do.

I didn’t set out intending to make a work like Nausicaä, so I doubt if I’ll ever make anything like it again.

—What’s on the horizon, now that you’ve finished serializing the Nausicaä manga?

Miyazaki: Having ended Nausicaä doesn’t mean that everything has ended or come to a conclusion. Things will continue, but we’ve come to the point where we all probably know how things will turn out. In other words, I ended the story at the same point as we are now, at the starting point of an incomprehensible world.

We can expect all sorts of ridiculous things to occur in the future, and people will make all sorts of efforts to overcome them. In Nausicaä, when it became clear that humans were destined to repeat the same things over and over, I finally tried to resolve the story.

While creating the story, I realized that the role of Nausicaä herself was not to become an actual leader or even a guide for her people. Rather, it was to act as a type of miko, a shaman-maiden who works at a Shinto shrine. But I agonized over this. Since it is not Nausicaä but the people who believe in her who move things along, from the perspective of traditional storytelling the story structure may not seem very logical.

Right now the story is supposed to be complete, but I still need to address a lot of issues, including those I have raised in this interview, before we put out the final paperback in the manga series. Still, I intend to end the story at this point, leaving what I don’t understand as unknowns.

If I don’t wrap things up now, this work—that I started back in my forties—will never, ever end, and I’ll never be able to peacefully transition into my old age. And to be quite frank, the moment I actually decided to finish the serialization, I already felt as though I had turned into a real wrinkled old geezer.

That stated, my work has by no means ended. And I’m really in a bind, because as a result I don’t truly feel liberated either. I wish I could say that I’ve just had a heavy load lifted from my shoulders. I thought life would be easier, but that isn’t the case. I thought that not having to continue the story anymore would make things easier for me, but instead what has happened is simply that the second-most difficult work I have has just moved up in rank, replacing Nausicaä as the most difficult work. [laughs]

—So the one thing that’s become clear is that lots of issues have piled up.

Miyazaki: That’s right. And that’s something that Nausicaä knows better than anyone.
